fig4_1: Line plot on the interval from minus one to one comparing the smooth bell-shaped Runge function (solid curve) against its polynomial interpolants (dashed curves) on equispaced nodes for degrees six, ten, and fourteen. The interpolants track the function in the center but develop progressively larger oscillations near the endpoints at x equals plus or minus one, with the swings ballooning as the degree rises, illustrating divergence.
fig4_2: Two side-by-side contour maps of the complex plane showing closed equipotential curves wrapping the real interval from minus one to one. Left, for uniform equispaced node density, the contours bulge only slightly off the real axis before reaching the Runge poles at z equals plus or minus zero point two i (marked by crosses). Right, for Chebyshev density, the equipotentials are nested Bernstein ellipses with foci at plus or minus one; the critical ellipse passing through the poles sets the convergence rate, and the contours enclose more of the plane, explaining why Chebyshev interpolation converges.
fig4_3: Geometric diagram of a unit semicircle with equally spaced points placed along its upper arc at angles theta sub j equal to j pi over N. Vertical dashed projection lines drop each circle point straight down to the x-axis, producing the Chebyshev nodes. Equal angular spacing on the arc maps to nodes that bunch together near the endpoints at x equals plus or minus one and spread out near the center, illustrating endpoint clustering.
fig4_4: Two-panel figure on Chebyshev interpolation of the Runge function. Left, a line plot from minus one to one shows the function and its interpolants for degrees six, ten, and fourteen lying almost on top of the function with no boundary oscillations. Right, the pointwise interpolation error on a logarithmic vertical axis drops sharply as the degree increases, the opposite of the equispaced case, confirming rapid convergence.
fig4_5: Two side-by-side line plots of the Lagrange basis polynomials L sub k for degree ten over the interval minus one to one, each curve equal to one at its own node and zero at the others. Left, on equispaced nodes the basis functions belonging to interior nodes swing to large positive and negative values near the boundaries. Right, on Chebyshev nodes every basis function stays small and bounded across the whole interval, showing far better behavior.
fig4_6: Two-panel figure on Lebesgue functions and constants. Left, the Lebesgue function for degree ten plotted over minus one to one for equispaced, Legendre, and Chebyshev nodes; the equispaced curve spikes to enormous peaks near the endpoints while the Legendre and Chebyshev curves stay low and gently rippled. Right, the Lebesgue constant versus degree N on a logarithmic vertical scale, with the equispaced curve rising as a steep straight line (exponential growth) and the Chebyshev curve nearly flat (logarithmic growth).
fig4_7: Semilogarithmic plot of the Lebesgue constant versus polynomial degree N comparing only Legendre and Chebyshev nodes, with the divergent equispaced curve omitted. The Legendre curve rises faster, consistent with order square root of N growth, while the Chebyshev curve grows most slowly, consistent with order log N, confirming Chebyshev nodes as the optimal choice among the two.
fig4_8: Semilogarithmic convergence plot of the maximum interpolation error against polynomial degree N for the Runge function. The Chebyshev curve (green) descends as a straight line, indicating geometric convergence at rate rho to the power minus N with rho about one point two two, while the equispaced curve (red) climbs steeply upward, indicating exponential divergence. The two curves move in opposite directions.
fig4_9: Semilogarithmic plot of the maximum Chebyshev interpolation error versus polynomial degree N for the Runge function, shown alone without the divergent equispaced curve. The error markers fall along a near-perfect descending straight line, the signature of geometric convergence at rate rho to the power minus N with rho about one point two two, matching the theoretical prediction from the pole locations at z equals plus or minus zero point two i.
fig4_10: Two-panel statistical figure for random nodes. Left, the Lebesgue constant versus polynomial degree N on a logarithmic vertical scale, with a solid mean curve rising steeply (exponential growth) and a wide shaded band marking the min-to-max range that broadens with N. Right, a histogram of the base-ten logarithm of the Lebesgue constant at degree fifteen over five hundred trials, spread across many orders of magnitude, with vertical reference lines marking the mean, median, equispaced, and Chebyshev values, the last two sitting far below most random outcomes.
fig4_11: Two-panel statistical figure for random Chebyshev nodes built from uniform random angles projected through cosine. Left, the Lebesgue constant versus polynomial degree N on a logarithmic vertical scale climbs explosively to astronomical values, with a shaded variability band spanning many orders of magnitude. Right, a histogram of the base-ten logarithm of the Lebesgue constant at degree fifteen over five hundred trials, extremely broad and shifted toward huge values, showing that despite the correct arcsine marginal these nodes perform catastrophically worse than every other distribution studied.
